lesson.title: Square Roots: Undoing the Squaring Power
lesson.summary: A square root asks what number, squared, gives back the value under the radical sign, making square roots the direct opposite operation of raising something to the power of 2.
lesson.body:
Raising a number to the power of 2 (squaring it) is one of the most familiar exponent operations there is: 6^2 means 6 times 6, which is 36. A square root reverses that exact process. The square root of a number b, written with the radical symbol as the square root of b, is the nonnegative number that gives b back when it is squared. So the square root of 36 is 6, because 6^2 = 36. This makes square roots and squaring inverse operations of each other, in the same way that subtraction undoes addition.

Certain numbers, called perfect squares, have square roots that come out to whole numbers, because they are exactly the square of a whole number. The first several perfect squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, and 144, coming from squaring 1 through 12. Recognizing these makes evaluating square roots much faster, since the square root of 64 is immediately 8 once you know 8^2 = 64, without needing to guess and check.

Square roots also work with fractions, following the same logic. The square root of the fraction 49 over 121 equals 7 over 11, because squaring 7 over 11 gives back 49 over 121: (7/11)^2 = 7^2 over 11^2 = 49 over 121. Checking the pieces individually, 7^2 = 49 and 11^2 = 121, confirming the square root is correct.

Not every number under a square root is a perfect square, and that is completely normal. The square root of 50 is not a whole number, but you can still pin down roughly where it falls by comparing it to nearby perfect squares. Since 49 is less than 50, which is less than 64, and the square root of 49 is 7 while the square root of 64 is 8, the square root of 50 must be between 7 and 8, specifically close to 7.07. This kind of estimating by bracketing between known perfect squares is a useful check whenever a calculator is not handy.

One detail is worth being precise about: the square root symbol, by convention, always refers to the nonnegative root, called the principal square root. This matters because the equation x^2 = 25 actually has two solutions, x = 5 and x = -5, since both 5^2 and (-5)^2 equal 25. But the expression "the square root of 25" by itself refers only to the positive value, 5. Also, since squaring any real number, positive or negative, always produces a result of zero or greater, there is no real number that squares to a negative value, which is why the square root of a negative number is not a real number.

It is worth pausing on why the square root undoes the power of 2 specifically, and not some other power, because that connection is what makes the two operations true inverses of each other. Squaring a number and then taking the square root of the result returns you to the original nonnegative number: for instance, start with 9, square it to get 81, and the square root of 81 is 9 again. Reversing the order works too, as long as the starting number is nonnegative: the square root of 16 is 4, and squaring 4 gives back 16. This round-trip behavior, going out and coming straight back, is exactly what it means for two operations to be inverses, and it is the same relationship that makes cube roots the inverse of raising a number to the power of 3, a connection the next lesson builds on directly.
